_note: 2.1.0 (over 2.0.0, which stays as it is): the slide titles and the speaker notes of the deck 3.1.0 (teach slides included), each slide tied to a concept by its example or its title; 46 slides tied.

slides.title: Debugging
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter teaches four instruments for finding bugs: raise, assert, logging and the debugger. Every concept comes with an idea, an everyday picture, a drawn mechanism, the code and what the run printed. The same examples run on the chapter page. Ask: which bug cost you the most time?

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: exceptions and tracebacks, assertions, logging, hunting bugs with the log, and the debugger. Each code example sits in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this same order. Example: part three holds six logging examples. Ask the class: which part do you expect to be hardest, and why?

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. First, which instrument fits which problem? Second, which printed outputs of the book differ in current Python? Example: a missing file calls for raise, a wrong total for the log. Ask the class to guess both answers before we reach the end.

slides.title: Part 1: Exceptions and tracebacks
slides.say: Part one. A function refuses a bad call with raise. The exception climbs the call stack, and the traceback is the report of that climb. Example: box print refuses a width of two. Ask the class: who should hear about a bad argument?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: errors and exceptions
slides.say: An exception is a fire alarm. Raise pulls the lever, and the traceback shows the path the alarm took through the building. Example: the stamp that refuses the wrong paper size. Ask the class to add one more everyday picture of their own for an error message.

slides.title: Story: the bug you can visit in a museum
slides.say: The logbook page is dated 9 September 1947, although a common file title wrongly says 1945. The moth was taped in beside a joke about the first actual case of a bug. Ask the class: what evidence do you keep when you debug?

slides.title: Raising exceptions: refuse a bad call
slides.say: A function that cannot serve a call should refuse it with raise. The exception carries a message to the caller. Example: a vending machine rejects a bent coin and shows why. Ask the class: why is a loud refusal better than a quietly wrong box?

slides.title: raise: a function refuses a bad call
slides.say: Read the three checks first, then the drawing lines. Four calls are in the table: three raise, one prints the box. Predict the box before the run. Ask the class: which message would you see for box_print of a star with width 2?

slides.title: The exception object: class, args, message
slides.say: An exception is an object with a class, args and a message. Except catches by class, and a child class is still caught by its parent. Example: ValueError is an Exception. Ask the class: which clause would catch both a KeyError and a ValueError?

slides.title: except ... as err: the exception object
slides.say: The first block shows the name, the args tuple and the message. The second shows that a ValueError is caught by except Exception. The tree in the picture is the reason. Ask the class: what would except ValueError do with a plain Exception?

slides.title: The traceback: the way an exception climbed
slides.say: When no function claims an exception, it climbs to the caller, and the traceback records the climb. Example: int fails inside read age, passes through load and ends at the try. Ask the class: which call is listed first, and why?

slides.title: The traceback: where an exception passed
slides.say: The chain is load, then read age, then int. Nobody inside claims the ValueError, so the try at the bottom catches it. The list names the frames, outermost first. Ask the class: what would the list show if load caught the error itself?

slides.title: Notes: context that travels with the error
slides.say: Since Python 3.11 an exception can carry notes. The code that knows the bigger task adds one and raises the same error again. Example: while reading the age field. Ask the class: why does a bare raise keep the original error?

slides.title: add_note: context travels with the error
slides.say: The inner except adds the note and re-raises. The outer except prints the notes and the last line of the formatted report. Compare the two lines in the table. Ask the class: where else could a useful note be added on the way up?

slides.title: Part 2: Assertions
slides.say: Part two. An assert is a tripwire for the programmer. It checks beliefs, not user input, and it disappears under python dash capital O. Example: a sorted list has its smallest age first. Ask the class: what is a belief in your last program?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: assertions
slides.say: An assertion is a tripwire set by the builder. It checks what must be true if the program is correct, and it guards the programmer, never the user. Example: testing a ladder before you climb it. Ask the class: which doorway in your last program deserves a tripwire?

slides.title: assert: an executable belief
slides.say: An assert states a belief and is silent while it holds. When it fails, Python raises AssertionError. Example: after sort, the first age is not larger than the last. Ask the class: which other belief about a sorted list could you assert?

slides.title: assert: a check the programmer believes
slides.say: Run it twice in your head: sorted, the assert passes; reversed, it fails with an empty message. The AssertionError is an ordinary exception, so it can be caught for the demo. Ask the class: why would a real program usually not catch it?

slides.title: assert for the programmer, raise for the user
slides.say: The user can pass an empty list, so we raise a ValueError. Only our own bug can make a negative total, so we assert. Example: a form field that is left empty. Ask the class: which of the two would you use for a typed age of minus five?

slides.title: assert for the programmer, raise for the user
slides.say: Three calls: a good list, an empty list and a list that breaks the sum. The table shows which statement fired and who could cause it. The assert message is built only on failure. Ask the class: what would happen under python dash O?

slides.title: python -O removes every assert
slides.say: Under python dash O, assert statements are removed before the program runs. That is why asserts guard the programmer and never the user. Example: a password check as an assert would vanish. Ask the class: what should guard a password instead?

slides.title: python -O removes every assert
slides.say: We compile the same text twice. The normal compile raises at the assert; with optimize equals one the assert is gone and the next line runs. No second program is needed to see it. Ask the class: what does __debug__ tell the program?

slides.title: Part 3: Logging
slides.say: Part three. Logging leaves a record without stopping the program. Choose a level, a format and a destination, and switch it off without deleting a line. Example: a ship's logbook. Ask the class: when did you last wish you had a log?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: logging
slides.say: A log is a logbook. Each entry has a level, the format is the form with blanks, and the file is the notebook. Disable is the mute button. Example: a flight recorder is always on and is read after the incident. Ask the class: what should such a record always contain?

slides.title: Story: the most effective debugging tool
slides.say: Kernighan wrote this in 1979 at Bell Labs. Thinking comes first, print statements second. Logging is the same idea with levels, files and an off switch. Example: a print that shows a total. Ask: when is a print statement enough?

slides.title: Story: a logging system with a birth certificate
slides.say: PEP 282 was created in February 2002 by Vinay Sajip and Trent Mick, and it landed in Python 2.3. The five levels are its design, and every logging example here uses them. Ask the class which level they would choose for a missing file.

slides.title: Logging levels: names with numbers
slides.say: Five names, five numbers, from ten to fifty. A message is shown when its number reaches the threshold. Example: a missing file is an ERROR, a finished step is INFO. Ask the class: which level is the default threshold, and what does it hide?

slides.title: Logging levels: five names, five numbers
slides.say: The first line prints the names with their numbers; the chart draws the same five bars. The second line shows that levels compare like numbers. Warning is greater than info. Ask the class: what does get level name of 40 return?

slides.title: basicConfig: one call sets up the log
slides.say: One call to basicConfig sets the threshold, the format and the place to write. With INFO the debug line stays silent. Example: a production run hears less than a test run. Ask the class: how would you hear the debug line again?

slides.title: basicConfig: choose what you hear
slides.say: Five calls, one per level, and four lines appear. Force equals true replaces an earlier set-up, so the example behaves the same on the page. The chart shows how many messages each threshold lets through. Ask the class: what changes at WARNING?

slides.title: The format string: the layout of one line
slides.say: The format string names the fields of a line: the time, the level and the message. Example: 91 percent disk full at a fixed minute. A fixed layout makes logs searchable. Ask the class: which field would you add to find the failing file?

slides.title: The format string: what each line shows
slides.say: To keep the result fixed, the record is built by hand with a fixed time and shown in UTC. In a real program logging builds the record for you. The drawing joins each placeholder to its value. Ask the class: why is a fixed time useful in a demo?

slides.title: filename=: the log on disk
slides.say: The named parameter filename sends the log to a file. The screen stays quiet and the evidence stays on disk. Example: a program that runs overnight. Ask the class: where would you look the next morning to see what happened?

slides.title: filename=: evidence on disk
slides.say: A temporary folder keeps the demo clean. Both messages land in the file, including the debug line, because the level is DEBUG. Reading the file afterwards shows both lines in the same format. Ask the class: what would change if the level were INFO?

slides.title: logging.disable: silence without deleting
slides.say: Disable silences a level and everything below it. Notset switches everything back on again. Example: quiet the whole program for a release without deleting a single call. Ask the class: why is this better than commenting out the logging lines?

slides.title: logging.disable: silence without deleting
slides.say: Four calls, and the table says which ones printed. After disable of critical even the error call is silent, because error is below critical. After notset it prints again. Predict each line before the run. Ask the class: what would disable of warning silence?

slides.title: Lazy formatting: build the text only if needed
slides.say: A message with arguments is formatted only if it is emitted. The f-string builds the text first, even when nobody reads it. Example: a baker who bakes only when a cake is ordered. Ask the class: when does this saving really matter in a big program?

slides.title: Arguments are formatted only when needed
slides.say: Loud counts how often Python turns it into text. With arguments the count stays at zero; the f-string adds one. The chart shows both counts. Both messages are below the INFO threshold. Ask the class: what would the count be at level DEBUG?

slides.title: Part 4: Hunting bugs with the log
slides.say: Part four. Three bugs from the chapter: a loop that starts too early, strings that were meant to be numbers, and a comparison that can never be true. Each is found by reading evidence. Ask the class: which of the three have you made yourself?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: hunting a bug
slides.say: Each of the three buggy programs hides one small mistake: a zero at the start, a string where a number belongs, a comparison across types. Example: gluing two number cards makes 53. Ask the class which of these pictures helps them most to remember the mistake.

slides.title: Hunting a bug with the log as witness
slides.say: Read the DEBUG lines: i starts at zero and the total dies with it. The log is the witness that shows the loop starts one step too early. Example: counting guests from the empty doorway. Ask the class: what did you expect on the first line?

slides.title: Hunt one bug with the log as witness
slides.say: Set the level, define the function with logging inside, call it for three. The chart and the table show total at every step. It is zero each time, so the answer is zero, not six. Ask the class: which single character would you change?

slides.title: The fix, and the log as proof
slides.say: Range from one to n plus one. The product grows one, two, six. The same log that found the bug now proves the fix. Example: checking the water meter after mending a tap. Ask the class: why rerun the same log and not just trust the result?

slides.title: The one-character fix, witnessed
slides.say: Only the range line differs from the buggy version. Compare the table with the previous slide: the totals now grow, and the last line says six. Same evidence, new result. Ask the class: what would factorial of zero give now?

slides.title: Text is not a number: the adding bug
slides.say: Input gives text, and plus joins text. Five, three and forty-two become 5342. Example: gluing number cards together. Convert each answer with int before adding. Ask the class: what would the sum be if only the first answer were converted?

slides.title: The string that beat the number
slides.say: The three variables stand in for typed answers. The first print joins them; the second converts and adds. The chart puts 5342 beside 50. Run it and compare the types in the table. Ask the class: why does input never return a number?

slides.title: A comparison that can never be true
slides.say: The toss is a number and the guess is a text. They are never equal, so the game never lets you win. Example: an apple compared with the word apple. Ask the class: which two values would make toss equal to guess?

slides.title: The coin toss that can never win
slides.say: The seed makes the toss repeatable. The first print shows both types and False. The loop shows that the tuple test only checks spelling, so maybe is rejected. The table lists every pair. Ask the class: does the tuple test fix the bug?

slides.title: Compare like with like
slides.say: Turn the number into its word before the comparison. Out of a thousand tosses the fixed game agrees about half the time; the buggy one never. Example: converting prices to one currency. Ask the class: why use a thousand games?

slides.title: Compare like with like
slides.say: Two counters, one loop, one print. The buggy comparison adds zero every time. The fixed one adds one when the word matches the guess. The chart compares the two totals. Ask the class: what total would you expect for a fair coin?

slides.title: Part 5: The debugger
slides.say: Part five. A debugger pauses the program and shows its variables. First see how it works inside, then the controls and the breakpoint call. Example: a pause button on a film. Ask the class: what do you want to see when the film stops?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the debugger
slides.say: A debugger pauses the film of the program. A breakpoint says where, and the inspector shows the variables while the film stands still. The Mu editor is where the book shows it. Example: watching cooking through the oven window. Ask the class: where would you put your first breakpoint?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the debugger controls
slides.say: Five controls: continue, step in, step over, step out and stop. Think of walking through a house: into a room, past a room, or back out to the hall. Ask the class which control they would use when the next line calls a function they already trust.

slides.title: The controls of the debugger
slides.say: The two functions are on the left, the controls on the right. Start at the line x equals add of two and three. Step in enters add, step over runs the line as a whole, step out finishes the function. Ask the class where each control pauses next.

slides.title: Inside a debugger: a hook on every line
slides.say: A debugger is a program that watches another program line by line. Settrace gives us the same hook in a few lines of code. Example: a projector with a pause button. Ask the class: what would a real debugger show at each pause?

slides.title: Inside a debugger: pause at every line
slides.say: Main calls add twice. Watch runs before every line and saves the function name and the local variables. The table is what an inspector pane would show at each pause. Read the first rows slowly. Ask the class: when does the variable x first appear?

slides.title: breakpoint() and the commands of pdb
slides.say: Breakpoint calls sys dot breakpointhook. Swap the hook and the call does something else; pdb offers the editor's controls as commands. Example: a red flag on the road. Ask the class: how would you switch every breakpoint off at once?

slides.title: breakpoint() and the commands of pdb
slides.say: We swap the hook for a print, call breakpoint, then restore the original hook. The last print checks which editor controls exist as pdb commands. The table maps each control to its command. Ask the class: which command leaves the debugger?

slides.title: Choose the instrument by the question
slides.say: Choose the instrument by the question. Can the caller fix it? Raise. Must it always be true? Assert. What happened during the run? Log. What is the state at this line? Debugger. Example: a negative total. Ask the class to choose the instrument for three problems.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. Notes arrived in 3.11, better error locations also in 3.11, and the safe attach to a running process in 3.14. The book does not cover these. Example: add note. Ask the class: which of these changes would help you most, and why?

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. Raise tells the caller why, assert states a belief, logging records, the log proves a fix, and a debugger pauses. The chart counts the examples of each part. Example: factorial. Ask the class to say the five sentences in their own words.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run on the page. Example: factorial of three with range of n plus one prints zero. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence, and to say which instrument they used and why it fits the problem.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation. The three stories link to first-hand sources. Example: PEP 282 is the birth certificate of the logging module. Choose one link and read it before the next class. Ask: which link will you open first?
